chunks: "I'd pick a concrete example so the numbers are consistent: 12 volts in, 3. 3 volts out, 2 amps, 4. 7 microhenries, 500 kilohertz. That's a duty cycle of 0.
275, so the high-side FET is on for 550 nanoseconds and off for 1. 45 microseconds. The switch node is the starting point.
It's 12 volts when the high-side FET is on, and about minus one diode drop when it's off, so it's a rectangular pulse whose average is 3. 3 volts.
With a synchronous bridge the off level is basically minus the low-side FET's I times R, near zero, with little negative dips during dead time when the body diode conducts.
The inductor voltage is the switch node minus V out : plus 8. 7 volts on, minus 3. 3 volts off. Integrate that and you get the inductor current, a triangle: rising at 1.
85 amps per microsecond, falling at 0. 7 amps per microsecond, about 1 amps peak to peak around the 2 amps average.
The capacitor current is the inductor current minus the load current, so the same triangle centred on zero.
Integrating that gives a small parabolic ripple, about 12 millivolts with some ESR. The load sees a nearly flat 3. 3 volts and 2 amps.
On the input side the current is only the high-side FET current: pulses of the inductor current for 550 nanoseconds and zero otherwise, average 0. 55 amps.
The input capacitor supplies the pulses.
The diode or low-side FET carries the inductor current during the off time, and the gate waveforms are the PWM, with the high-side gate bootstrapped above V in ."
